title: Saaty school selection example (three high schools, six criteria)
description: One of the earliest published AHP applications: Saaty and his son ranked three high schools against six criteria. The criteria matrix is a well-known example of a strongly inconsistent judgment matrix (lambda_max about 7.42 for n = 6; CR about 0.23 under Saaty's RI). Expected values are derived with the principal-eigenvector method from the published matrices. Note that on this example the final ranking of schools A and B differs between the principal-eigenvector synthesis (B slightly ahead of A) and the column-normalization approximation (A slightly ahead of B) - see the synthesis alternate; the margin is about 0.01 either way, so implementations using different documented prioritization methods can legitimately report different top choices on this fixture.

source.citation: T. L. Saaty, 'A scaling method for priorities in hierarchical structures', Journal of Mathematical Psychology 15(3), 1977, pp. 234-281 (the school selection example); matrices as reproduced in N. Krivulin, 'Tropical implementation of the analytical hierarchy process decision method', arXiv:1802.01989, Section 5.2.

scale.name: saaty-1-9
scale.notes: Judgments on Saaty's fundamental 1-9 scale; reciprocals (e.g. 1/3) and intermediate or fractional values are valid entries. Matrix entries may be given as numbers or as fraction strings such as "1/3".

ri_table.name: saaty
ri_table.source: T. L. Saaty, The Analytic Hierarchy Process, McGraw-Hill, 1980. Values as tabulated in J. A. Alonso and M. T. Lamata, 'Consistency in the analytic hierarchy process: a new approach', International Journal of Uncertainty, Fuzziness and Knowledge-Based Systems 14(4), 2006, Table 1 (Wharton column).

matrices.description: Importance of the six criteria for choosing a school.
